items.prompt: Which structure receives input from other cells and carries it toward the neuron's integration region?

choices.a: Dendrites
choices.b: Myelin nodes

items.rationale: Dendrites and the cell body receive influences that are integrated near the start of the axon.

targetedFeedback.b: Nodes regenerate action potentials along a myelinated axon rather than serving as the main receptive branches.
targetedFeedback.c: The synaptic cleft is the gap between cells, not a neuron structure that carries input inward.
targetedFeedback.d: The adrenal cortex is endocrine tissue.

items.prompt: During repolarization of a typical action potential, which ion movement is most important?

choices.a: K⁺ leaves through voltage-gated potassium channels.
choices.b: Na⁺ enters through every leak channel.

items.rationale: Delayed opening of voltage-gated potassium channels allows K⁺ efflux, moving membrane voltage back toward a negative value.

targetedFeedback.b: Rapid sodium entry produces depolarization rather than repolarization.
targetedFeedback.c: Synaptic calcium concerns transmitter release, not the main axonal falling phase.
targetedFeedback.d: Glucose transport is unrelated to repolarization of the neuron membrane.

items.prompt: Which division carries sensory input and motor output outside the brain and spinal cord?

choices.a: Peripheral nervous system
choices.b: Central nervous system

items.rationale: Peripheral nerves connect receptors and effectors with the central nervous system.

targetedFeedback.b: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord rather than the nerves outside them.
targetedFeedback.c: The endocrine system communicates through hormones in blood.
targetedFeedback.d: The lymphatic system has different transport and immune functions.

items.prompt: Which pair contains sensory receptor cells?

choices.a: Retinal rods and cochlear hair cells
choices.b: Lens fibres and auditory ossicles

items.rationale: Rods transduce light, and cochlear hair cells transduce mechanical vibration into receptor signals.

targetedFeedback.b: The lens focuses light and ossicles transmit vibration; neither is the receptor cell named here.
targetedFeedback.c: The optic nerve carries neural output and the tube equalizes pressure.
targetedFeedback.d: The iris controls pupil size, while fluid motion stimulates receptors but is not itself a receptor cell.

items.prompt: What makes a cell a target for a particular hormone?

choices.a: It has a compatible receptor and response pathway.
choices.b: It is closest to the gland.

items.rationale: Hormone response depends on receptor binding and intracellular machinery, not simply physical distance from the gland.

targetedFeedback.b: Hormones travel in blood, so proximity alone does not define target status.
targetedFeedback.c: Many hormone targets are non-neural tissues.
targetedFeedback.d: Cells require membranes; the claim does not explain hormone specificity.

items.prompt: Which pancreatic cell-hormone pairing is correct?

choices.a: Alpha cell—glucagon
choices.b: Beta cell—PTH

items.rationale: Pancreatic alpha cells release glucagon; beta cells release insulin.

targetedFeedback.b: PTH is released by parathyroid glands.
targetedFeedback.c: ADH is synthesized in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.
targetedFeedback.d: Thyroxine is produced by the thyroid gland.

items.prompt: Which statement distinguishes negative feedback from positive feedback?

choices.a: Negative feedback reduces the initiating departure; positive feedback amplifies it.
choices.b: Negative feedback is harmful and positive feedback is healthy.
choices.c: Only hormones can create negative feedback.
choices.d: Positive feedback always keeps a variable near a stable range.

items.rationale: The terms describe the direction of the response's effect on the initiating change, not whether the response is good or bad.

targetedFeedback.b: Positive and negative describe direction, not value or health.
targetedFeedback.c: Neural, endocrine, and integrated pathways can produce negative feedback.
targetedFeedback.d: Positive feedback amplifies change and is usually bounded by an external stop condition.

items.prompt: A stimulus reaches −54 mV when threshold is −55 mV. What should occur if voltage-gated channels function normally?

choices.a: A full action potential begins.
choices.b: A half-height action potential begins.
choices.c: The membrane remains permanently at −54 mV.

items.rationale: Crossing threshold triggers regenerative sodium-channel opening and an all-or-none action potential.

targetedFeedback.b: Action-potential amplitude is not proportional to how far threshold is crossed.
targetedFeedback.c: Channel changes drive voltage through the action-potential sequence rather than leaving it fixed.
targetedFeedback.d: A threshold crossing does not convert synaptic transmitters into endocrine hormones.

items.prompt: A toxin inhibits acetylcholinesterase. Which immediate synaptic change is expected?

choices.a: Acetylcholine remains in the cleft longer and receptors are stimulated for longer.
choices.b: Acetylcholine can no longer be released from any terminal.
choices.c: Sodium-potassium pumps disappear from all neurons.

items.rationale: Cholinesterase normally terminates acetylcholine action, so inhibition prolongs transmitter presence and receptor stimulation.

targetedFeedback.b: The toxin affects breakdown rather than the release step described.
targetedFeedback.c: Pump disappearance is not the mechanism of cholinesterase inhibition.
targetedFeedback.d: Synaptic enzyme inhibition does not rapidly increase myelin thickness.

items.prompt: A local anesthetic blocks sensory action potentials from a finger. Which part of a withdrawal pathway fails first?

choices.a: Afferent information does not reach central integration normally.
choices.b: The motor neuron becomes an endocrine gland.
choices.c: The muscle can no longer contain actin.
choices.d: The hypothalamus stops releasing every hormone.

items.rationale: Blocking sensory axon conduction reduces the input reaching spinal integration, even if motor neurons and muscle remain capable of responding.

targetedFeedback.b: Cell identity does not change because conduction is blocked.
targetedFeedback.c: The anesthetic effect is on sensory signalling, not muscle structural proteins.
targetedFeedback.d: A local sensory block does not stop all hypothalamic endocrine control.

items.prompt: An object is clear at distance but blurry when close. Which process should be examined first?

choices.a: Lens accommodation and ciliary-muscle control
choices.b: Cochlear fluid movement

items.rationale: Near focus requires accommodation: ciliary-muscle action changes lens shape and refractive power.

targetedFeedback.b: Cochlear fluid is part of hearing.
targetedFeedback.c: PTH regulates calcium and does not directly focus the lens.
targetedFeedback.d: A spinal reflex is not the optical focusing mechanism.

items.prompt: An audiogram threshold changes from 10 dB to 35 dB at one frequency. How should the change be interpreted?

choices.a: A greater sound level was needed for detection at that frequency.
choices.b: Hearing became more sensitive at that frequency.
choices.d: The graph alone identifies the exact cause.

items.rationale: A higher threshold indicates lower sensitivity for that test frequency, but it does not by itself establish the mechanism.

targetedFeedback.b: Greater required level means reduced, not improved, sensitivity.
targetedFeedback.c: The result concerns hearing rather than retinal anatomy.
targetedFeedback.d: Cause requires additional clinical and pathway evidence.

items.prompt: A warm stimulus feels less intense after remaining constant for a minute. Which explanation best fits?

choices.a: Sensory adaptation reduces the response to an unchanging stimulus.
choices.b: All thermoreceptors have died.
choices.c: The stimulus changed from heat to light.

items.rationale: Many sensory pathways reduce firing during a constant stimulus, emphasizing change; this does not mean all receptors stopped functioning permanently.

targetedFeedback.b: Reduced perception during a constant safe stimulus is not evidence of cell death.
targetedFeedback.c: The stimulus modality remains thermal.
targetedFeedback.d: Insulin is not the mechanism described for short-term sensory adaptation.

items.prompt: A posterior-pituitary lesion prevents hormone release while hypothalamic synthesis continues. Which blood hormone would be directly reduced?

choices.a: ADH
choices.b: Insulin

items.rationale: ADH is synthesized by hypothalamic neurons and normally released from their terminals in the posterior pituitary.

targetedFeedback.b: Insulin is synthesized and released by pancreatic beta cells.
targetedFeedback.c: PTH is released by parathyroid glands.
targetedFeedback.d: Thyroxine is produced by the thyroid gland.

items.prompt: Blood calcium is high. Which immediate change is consistent with negative feedback in the PTH pathway?

choices.a: PTH release decreases.
choices.b: PTH release increases to raise calcium further.
choices.d: The parathyroid glands become sensory neurons.

items.rationale: High calcium reduces the stimulus for PTH secretion, limiting responses that would otherwise raise calcium.

targetedFeedback.b: Increasing PTH would tend to amplify the high-calcium departure in the simplified model.
targetedFeedback.c: Hormones do not transform into one another.
targetedFeedback.d: Endocrine cells can sense variables without becoming neurons.

items.prompt: During fasting, glucose falls and glucagon rises. Which target response helps oppose the fall?

choices.a: The liver increases glycogen breakdown and glucose release.
choices.b: Every brain cell requires insulin before using glucose.
choices.d: Muscle exports large amounts of free glucose from glycogen directly into blood.

items.rationale: Glucagon acts strongly on the liver to increase glucose availability and release into blood.

targetedFeedback.b: Brain glucose transport is not insulin-dependent in the same way as many muscle and adipose responses.
targetedFeedback.c: Insulin is released by pancreatic beta cells.
targetedFeedback.d: Muscle glycogen supports local muscle metabolism; the liver is the principal direct source of free blood glucose in this model.

items.prompt: Five minutes after a startling event, epinephrine is high but cortisol has barely changed. Which pathway best explains the immediate phase?

choices.a: Sympathetic activation of the adrenal medulla
choices.b: A completed long-duration HPA response

items.rationale: The timing and epinephrine pattern fit rapid sympathetic-adrenal-medulla activation better than the slower cortisol axis.

targetedFeedback.b: Cortisol has barely changed, so the slower HPA pathway cannot best explain the immediate peak.
targetedFeedback.c: The thyroid axis does not explain this alarm-timing evidence.
targetedFeedback.d: Calcium regulation is unrelated to the immediate startle pattern.

items.prompt: ADH rises but aldosterone remains near baseline after a salty meal with adequate water. Which distinction helps explain the pattern?

choices.a: ADH responds strongly to osmotic concentration, while aldosterone is regulated mainly by volume-related kidney signals and potassium.
choices.b: ADH and aldosterone are the same hormone.
choices.d: ADH directly transports sodium through every tissue.

items.rationale: ADH and aldosterone overlap in fluid regulation but respond to different inputs and change different kidney processes.

targetedFeedback.b: They are distinct hormones with different sources and targets.
targetedFeedback.c: Aldosterone acts mainly in kidney sodium handling, not phototransduction.
targetedFeedback.d: ADH primarily changes collecting-duct water permeability rather than sodium transport in every tissue.

items.prompt: A graph has time on the horizontal axis and hormone concentration on the vertical axis. What should be done before choosing a mechanism?

choices.a: Read units, identify baseline and trends, and compare the timing of variables.
choices.b: Choose the most familiar hormone name.
choices.c: Ignore values that do not fit the first idea.

items.rationale: Accurate data interpretation begins with axes, units, baseline, magnitude, and timing before a mechanism is selected.

targetedFeedback.b: Familiarity does not connect the mechanism to the supplied evidence.
targetedFeedback.c: Contradictory data should prompt model revision, not deletion.
targetedFeedback.d: Timing and association can support a hypothesis but do not alone establish causation.

items.prompt: Two axons produce action potentials of the same amplitude, but Axon B fires four times as often. Which inference is strongest?

choices.a: Axon B can represent a stronger or changing stimulus through firing frequency without taller spikes.
choices.b: Axon B has lost the all-or-none property.
choices.c: Axon A must be endocrine tissue.
choices.d: The sodium-potassium pump made Axon B's individual spikes smaller.

items.rationale: Stimulus intensity can be encoded by spike frequency and recruitment while each action potential remains all-or-none.

targetedFeedback.b: Similar spike amplitude is consistent with all-or-none behaviour.
targetedFeedback.c: Both are described as axons and use neural signalling.
targetedFeedback.d: The evidence states equal spike amplitude and does not support this pump claim.

items.prompt: A two-point threshold study compares fingertips tested first with forearms tested second for every participant. Which design change best addresses an order effect?

choices.a: Counterbalance which body region is tested first across participants.
choices.b: Use a different spacing scale for every person.
choices.c: Tell participants the correct response before each trial.

items.rationale: Counterbalancing distributes practice and fatigue effects across conditions, making region differences easier to interpret.

targetedFeedback.b: Inconsistent distances reduce comparability.
targetedFeedback.c: Providing the expected answer biases the measurement.
targetedFeedback.d: Post hoc deletion does not control systematic order effects.

items.prompt: Case X has low thyroxine/high TSH; Case Y has low thyroxine/low TSH. Which explanation best compares them?

choices.a: X points toward a thyroid-level limitation, while Y makes inadequate hypothalamic or pituitary drive a candidate.
choices.b: Both prove the same thyroid disorder.
choices.d: TSH provides no information about pathway location.

items.rationale: Pairing target-gland output with pituitary drive helps localize candidate pathway levels while remaining non-diagnostic.

targetedFeedback.b: Different TSH patterns suggest different candidate locations.
targetedFeedback.c: Low TSH indicates low measured pituitary drive, not excess stimulation.
targetedFeedback.d: TSH is useful when interpreted with thyroxine and context.

items.prompt: A synthetic urine sample contains glucose and ketones after a prolonged glucose elevation. Which conclusion is appropriately bounded?

choices.a: The pattern is consistent with disrupted fuel regulation and justifies additional clinical evidence; it is not diagnostic alone.
choices.b: The pattern proves a specific diabetes type.
choices.c: The kidneys caused every glucose change.
choices.d: Medication should be changed immediately from this course result.

items.rationale: Urine evidence can indicate a pattern for further investigation but cannot establish diagnosis, type, cause, or treatment by itself.

targetedFeedback.b: Diabetes type requires additional physiological and clinical evidence.
targetedFeedback.c: The kidneys handle filtered substances, but this pattern does not prove they caused the metabolic disturbance.
targetedFeedback.d: Classroom evidence must not be used to direct personal treatment changes.

items.prompt: In an integrated case, heart activity peaks at 5 minutes, cortisol at 45 minutes, and ADH after two hours without fluid. Which model is strongest?

choices.a: Different disturbances recruit overlapping neural and endocrine pathways on different time scales.
choices.b: One hormone caused every observation at the same moment.
choices.c: The data prove a chronic disorder.
choices.d: Timing is irrelevant when variables are measured.

items.rationale: The staggered evidence supports rapid neural/adrenal-medulla control, slower HPA-axis activity, and later water-balance feedback rather than one universal cause.

targetedFeedback.b: The distinct time courses and signals contradict a single simultaneous cause.
targetedFeedback.c: A short synthetic case does not establish chronic disease.
targetedFeedback.d: Timing is essential for distinguishing candidate mechanisms.
